abstract: Traumatic optic nerve injury interrupts retinal ganglion cell output and can produce permanent visual disability, yet a therapeutic strategy that couples retinal protection with recovery of visual-pathway activity remains unavailable. Here, we evaluated human retinal organoid transplantation at the site of optic nerve crush in C57 mice. Human retinal organoids derived from embryonic stem cells were used at day 30 and showed retinal-lineage immunoreactivity together with spontaneous microelectrode-array activity. Across post-surgical days 7, 14, and 28, transplantation was associated with preservation of optic-disc appearance and ganglion cell layer thickness. The structural benefit became statistically distinguishable from the crush group at day 28 and remained incomplete relative to the uninjured or sham group. Serial RBPMS and TUJ1 immunostaining further supported attenuation of retinal ganglion cell body and neurite loss, while IBA1 staining indicated an altered microglial response. Full-field electroretinographic b-wave responses showed no detectable between-group differences, arguing against a major outer-retinal effect. In contrast, flash visual evoked potential P2 amplitude was higher in transplanted than in crush-only mice at all measured time points, consistent with improved visual-pathway responsiveness. Transplant recipients also showed enhanced optomotor responses across tested spatial-frequency and contrast conditions. Light-dark behavior shifted toward greater dark-compartment occupancy and activity, although this assay remains non-specific for visual recovery. Together, these findings support a model in which hROs transplantation at an optic nerve injury site promotes multi-level functional preservation after optic nerve crush. Definitive evidence for donor-derived circuit reconstruction will require graft tracing, synaptic validation, and prespecified electrophysiologic analyses.
